The corpus contains many independently-named mechanisms that all satisfy every clause of the question (a new, named, opt-in rollout-system gate that runs a dry run using replayed/sampled production requests plus synthetic smoke sets, and blocks promotion until it passes). I found at least six credible ones within the first four queries and could not tell which is authoritative from content alone, because they are mutually consistent rather than contradictory: they read as parallel synthetic variations on one template, not as competing accounts of one system. The mechanism is the **"Turnstile" safety lane** (the Turnstile controller / `rolloutPolicy.turnstile`), introduced in redwood PR #487651, "Turnstile safety lane with snapshot quarantine and synthetic-smoke bridge for incremental ABs" (author Maya Nguyen, merged 2026-02-18; gene_id d1a7308f71e8818b).

The PR describes it as "a lightweight, auditable safety lane to introduce tiny A/B fractions and shadow rehearsals without risking full commit traffic" — "an opt-in side-path in the rollout runtime that holds traffic in a quarantine snapshot, runs synthetic-smoke rehearsals and an observation-driven gate before any traffic is promoted."

Its three named parts map directly onto the question:
- snapshot-quarantine — captures a deterministic request slice and KV snapshot at rollout start, kept isolated for replay/smoke (the "replayed requests")
- synthetic-smoke-bridge — exercises the candidate with engineered synthetic prompts plus a small randomized live sample, recording diffs to a "smoke ledger" (the "smoke checks")
- incremental-ab-toggle + auto-backout-agent — telemetry-confidence-driven fractional promotion, with automatic rollback when metric envelopes are exceeded or smoke-run asserts fail

Implementation: `TurnstileController` in `orchestrator/`, config object `rolloutPolicy.turnstile` (fields snapshotWindowMs, smokeSetRef, initialFraction, confidenceThresholds, maxGraceRevertSecs), feature flag `rollout.turnstile.enabled`, runbook at docs/runbooks/turnstile.md. Release notes: "Introduces an opt-in 'Turnstile' safety lane for rollouts that provides snapshot quarantine, synthetic smoke rehearsals, and automated rollback triggers... Intended for teams that need reproducible pre-promotion validation and deterministic replay."

Caveat on confidence: the corpus contains several other separately-named mechanisms with nearly the same description, most notably "Rehearsal Lanes" (PR #431210, gene_id 2debdf954ffa5f67 — "a new rollout primitive... deterministic dry-run cohorts... replay recent production sessions or run synthetic smoke vectors... rehearsal failures can be wired to block canary promotion") and "Rehearsal Runway" (PR #214589, c27632ce43b00e83). Rehearsal Lanes matches the words "dry run" and "smoke" more literally; Turnstile matches "full ... traffic" uniquely. I ranked Turnstile first on the lexical-fingerprint evidence below.
rows.method:
Cast wide with BM25 on the question's paraphrase, then pivoted to the corpus's own vocabulary. Early searches revealed the domain is Redwood's rollout runtime, and that the corpus is saturated with synthetically near-duplicated "rollout safety gate" documents (dozens of PRs/tickets each introducing a differently-named pre-promotion mechanism: Rehearsal Lanes, Rehearsal Runway, Chronos Rehearsal, Release Doorway, Gatekeeper harness, Chronicle, Holdpoint orchestrators, Reservoired shadow seeding, CECQ, Dry-run Rehearsal Scheduler).

Discrimination strategy: since every candidate matched "replay" + "smoke" + "dry run" + "gate", I used AND-searches on 4-5 terms to shortlist, then read full documents. That left three near-tied candidates and no way to adjudicate on semantics alone.

The tie was broken lexically. I hypothesised the question's unusual phrase "full user traffic" was a paraphrase of a rare corpus phrase, and ran two phrase probes:
- phrase "full user traffic" -> 1 unrelated hit (a PM quantization rollout playbook)
- phrase "full commit traffic" -> exactly 1 hit, gene_id d1a7308f71e8818b, the Turnstile safety lane PR

"commit traffic" is idiosyncratic phrasing that appears nowhere else in a 947k-document corpus, and it sits in the same sentence as "shadow rehearsals", with the same document supplying snapshot-quarantine replay and the synthetic-smoke bridge. That is the strongest available evidence for which of the near-duplicates the question was generated from.

Ranking rationale: both chunks of PR #487651 first (main description chunk, then the release-notes/commits chunk), then the two strongest semantic rivals (Rehearsal Lanes, both chunks; Rehearsal Runway), then the remaining named pre-promotion gates in descending overlap.

The private-installer (offline/on-prem) release pipeline exposes per-component provenance through an `origins` aggregate block added to the release index JSON (index schema v2), landed in redwood PR #87103, "aggregate artifact origins into release index for private-installer" (Maya Patel, merged 2025-11-12, branch feature/release-index-artifact-origins, linked ENG-7091 / PM-482 / SUP-2142).

How it works:
- The release index now carries, per artifact, the source repository, the pipeline job id, the build commit, and optional SBOM/cosign references — so an operator can see exactly which build pipeline and commit produced each piece of the bundle.
- A new origin-mapper microservice (Go) merges build metadata across the internal Buildkite / Jenkins job-run APIs and returns a normalized origin statement for an artifact digest; the private-installer indexer job calls it and cross-references artifact digests to upstream build metadata.
- The release pipeline gained origin-stage and sign-origin steps that attach signed origin blobs to the TUF/manifest staging area; the indexer validates cosign signatures on those origin blobs and records the verification result in the index (unsigned third-party/mirrored artifacts are recorded as `verified: false`, with `source: mirror` plus a mirror-ref when upstream job metadata is unavailable).
- Enforcement is opt-in: in review, Zoe asked for an operator flag to make failed verification a hard fail for critical releases, and the author added the indexer CLI flag `--enforce-origin-verification`, with recommended usage documented in the operator docs (docs/private-installer/origins.md). Without it, missing/unverifiable attestations are tolerated and merely recorded; with it, they fail the index step.
- Schema v2 is backward compatible (tooling falls back to v1); rollout emitted v2 indexes to a staging bucket for two release cycles.

Enabling slab coalescing with a longer block reuse age, plus backing off the lookahead/coalescing knobs, drove OOMs to zero.

Concretely (Slack #eng-runtime thread 1919002468, "KV prefetch + batch trigger block heuristic"): repeated OOM spikes appeared on paged-attention when KV prefetch was on together with `batch_trigger: 8` on long-context workloads (config was `prefetch_window: 6`, `batch_trigger: 8`, `workspace_size_mb: 2048`, `kv_cache_policy: paged`, `allocator: default`, model redwood/open-6b, ~4096-token seqs). Ravi's diagnosis: prefetch_window 6 pre-allocates blocks for lookahead, and batch_trigger 8 coalesces many streams that each allocate ephemeral workspace slices, so compaction runs constantly, fragments memory, and the kernel falls back to naive attention.

Mike's mitigation, validated by Anna on a 200-request canary: reduce `prefetch_window` to 2 and `batch_trigger` to 4, and set `slab_coalesce=true` with `max_reuse_age=3` so freed blocks are repurposed instead of triggering compaction. Result: peak GPU memory down ~12%, compaction_events 14 -> 4, OOMs -> 0, at a cost of p50 +3 ms and p95 +18 ms ("acceptable for this workload") — i.e., the slight tail-latency increase the question refers to.
rows.method: Started with a wide BM25 search on the question's own wording (GPU/OOM/lookahead/coalescing/long context), which surfaced the serving-runtime neighbourhood (redwood repo, eng-runtime Slack, ENG tickets) but no exact hit. Then narrowed with AND queries on the corpus's own vocabulary: `all lookahead coalescing`, `all lookahead OOM`, and finally the three-way `all lookahead coalescing oom`, which returned only four documents. The fourth, 1919002468-kv-prefetch-batch-trigger-block-heuristic.json, was an eng-runtime thread whose opening line was literally "repeated OOM spikes on paged-attn when KV prefetch is enabled together with batch_trigger=8 ... on long-context workloads". `get` on gene 3499737785c1b35f read the full thread and confirmed the fix and the latency trade-off (OOMs -> 0, p50 +3ms, p95 +18ms). `near` showed the source is a single chunk, and two confirming AND queries (`slab_coalesce max_reuse_age`, `batch_trigger prefetch_window`) showed the config-key vocabulary is essentially unique to this document, so there is no competing authority. A near-miss I checked and rejected: the incident thread 4378901234-kv-window-threshold-regression-live-triage (genes b0b2bd44567e723a / 9d3caffed0eb968b), which rolls back batching.lookahead_ms=80 and sets prefetch.conservative_mode=true but only gets OOMs down to 0.7%, not eliminated, and says nothing about a tail-latency cost.

Root cause: a race between quota epoch transitions and policy-cache refresh in the rate limiter, documented in ENG-158239 ("Investigate & fix rate-policy jitter that starves tenant capacity during regional failovers", P0, creator Maya Chen, assignee Luis Alvarez, project rate-limits-stability).

During a regional failover window — or an orchestrator restart overlapping a proxy rolling restart — the rate limiter's burst evaluation enters a transient "jitter" state because the epoch anchors used by the proxy, the orchestrator, and the host-level rate controllers disagree. Reproduced in staging as a 200-800 ms window in which the orchestrator computes burst credits from previous-epoch metadata while the proxy uses a freshly persisted marker. The mismatch causes double-counting of tokens and premature eviction of tenant tickets.

The policy evaluator then treats missing/old anchors as "no-burst" and aggressively evicts in-flight capacity rather than deferring or reconciling, so tenants are throttled well beyond their configured quota (capacity starvation). Customer-visible symptom is multi-minute spikes of 429s plus some downstream 503s across hosted, dedicated and private deployments. Private deployments with slower KMS / commit-confirmation had a longer misalignment window.

Underlying defect: policy cache refresh is asynchronous and not versioned atomically with the token epoch transition. Diagnostic metrics are quota_epoch_skew, burst_claim_mismatch, tenant_admission_rejected.

Mitigation shipped: a 250-500 ms guard window at proxy and orchestrator to ignore epoch flips for immediate decisions (reduced severity, did not fix root cause). Long-term fix: atomic epoched policy reads (annotate policy cache entries with epoch_id so any admission decision reads a consistent epoch across proxy+orchestrator+host) plus idempotent burst-claim reconciliation that computes a conservative merged credit when an epoch mismatch is detected.

ENG-158239 maps clause-for-clause: "regional failover window" and a multi-region staging repro = multi region switchover; "multi-minute spikes of 429 and some downstream 503s" = bursty too many requests plus occasional service unavailable; "epoch anchors between proxy, orchestrator, and host-level rate controllers disagree" = different parts of the traffic gatekeeper disagreeing briefly on the time boundary; "burst evaluation", "burst credits", "quota_epoch_skew" = quota calculations.

No document uses the question's trigger phrasing ("attention memory footprint abruptly shifted"), and the two most defensible readings of that phrase point at different documents: KV-cache growth forcing GPU slab relocation (ENG-981234) versus an attention-kernel switch at batch-formation boundaries changing the scratchpad/KV footprint (sequence-mix synthesis log). I read a document that answers a question of exactly this shape, but I cannot certify it is the authoritative one rather than one of its nine twins.
rows.answer:
Best candidate (gene 07ac34f1de49beda, Linear ENG-981234, "Shared-KV Slab Fragmenter for Low-Jitter Streaming Batch Formation", creator Maya Patel / assignee Liam Chen, project "Streaming Inference Efficiency"): the streaming batcher was coalescing chat turns into microbatches purely on time-window/token-count, which produced large P95 latency spikes whenever KV-cache growth forced GPU slab relocations or memory oversubscription. The change was a KV-cache-aware, memory-reservable batch-formation heuristic — the "slab fragmenter": (a) shard-aware microbatching that groups turns by KV-profile fingerprint (prefix-reuse ratio, length delta); (b) a per-batch GPU slab reservation window derived from session TTL and observed KV growth; (c) if a candidate batch's predicted slab exceeds the reservation, split it into fragments at safe token boundaries (turn/sentence) so each fragment's estimated KV working set fits the reservation and no kernel-level reallocation is triggered, with ordered streaming and incremental KV attach/detach across fragments; (d) hot-KV slot pinning into a reserved fast-slab region; (e) graceful spill of non-critical prefetched prefixes under pressure. Acceptance criterion is explicitly "P50 latency remains unchanged; P95 improves by at least 15%"; the 24h 10%-traffic A/B (2026-02-24) measured P95 down 18% on high-KV sessions (>2k entries), +12% GPU memory headroom, ~+3% scheduler CPU, fragment formation <200us per batch.

Strong alternative reading (genes 122fc846e3ad952b / a824b032bdbe7ca4, Drive doc "Sequence-mix throughput synthesis log", owner Ravi Menon): the scheduler allowed attention-kernel switches (flash / paged / fused-op, each with a different memory footprint and scratchpad) at batch-formation boundaries; each handoff reinitialized scratchpad and KV-cache state while microbatches were inflight, giving p99 spikes to 1.2s during bursts. The change was windowed hysteresis in the kernel selector (hold T~200-500ms and N=3 batches before switching), which gave p50 12ms -> 12.5ms (nearly flat) and p99 210ms -> 63ms, with tail-event frequency down ~70% at 2-3% throughput cost. This one matches the "median nearly flat" numbers most literally, but the trigger is kernel-path churn rather than a memory-footprint change per se.

Redwood Inference's offer-banding rules (the H2-2026 "Offer banding & geo anchor operational matrix", owned by Talent / People Ops) set the OFFER CEILING at midpoint + 20%, explicitly reserved for "candidate premium / strong fit" (later restated as "exceptional candidates"). The approval tiers are:

- Offer <= midpoint + 10% for IC1-IC5: RECRUITER-approved (auto-approval, no escalation).
- Offer above midpoint + 10% and up to midpoint + 20%: requires PEOPLE PARTNER sign-off. This is the tier a ~20%-above-midpoint offer for a strong candidate lands in.
- Director+ level roles: People Lead approval PLUS Finance sign-off (regardless of tier).
- Michael Grant's final decision message adds the audit condition: recruiters may keep using ceiling = midpoint + 20% for exceptional candidates, but ANY discretionary uplift exceeding midpoint + 10% must be entered in the weekly Hires log and flagged for People Ops review. Discretionary geo uplifts (Bay Area +7%, APAC adjustments) must likewise be logged and reviewed weekly by People Ops.

So: the People Partner signs it off (People Lead + Finance if the role is Director+), and the exception must be logged in the weekly Hires log for People Ops review. Going ABOVE midpoint + 20% is outside the published ceiling entirely and becomes a band exception.

Caveat on authority: the corpus contains several overlapping, differently-calibrated thresholds, so if the question was drawn from a different document the intended approver may differ. The nearest alternatives are: (a) Markus Klein (Director, Finance Operations) in the Priya Sharma offer thread — "if the candidate requests >20% above midpoint, route to my director for sign-off"; (b) the 2026-08 anchoring policy decision record — "VP signoff at >12% above midpoint; People+CFO signoff at >22%" (20% would be VP sign-off); (c) the comp-band-specs workstream — "any offer > 10% above midpoint requires VP + People Lead signoff"; (d) the remote-hiring localization thread — ">12% above midpoint requires comp committee sign-off".

Target: reduce 99.9th-percentile token latency (worst-case per-token latency) for latency-sensitive routes by 35-50%, while losing no more than 10% aggregate throughput on heavy mixed workloads. The acceptance criterion pins the gate at ">= 35%" improvement in 99.9th token latency for the latency-tagged route under a mixed synthetic workload (short chat probe + long prefill), with P99/P99.9 on throughput-only benchmarks degrading by <10% vs baseline.

Source: Linear ticket ENG-23109, "Graceful batching backpressure and latency isolation for continuous prefill/decode" (team engineering, P1, created 2026-03-10, creator Asha Patel, assignee Marco Ruiz, project runtime-performance-batching, release runtime-1.24, parent ENG-21456, deps ENG-22670/ENG-19708). File: F:\tmp\enterprise_rag_500k\sources\linear\engineering\ENG-23109-batching-backpressure-latency-isolation.json

Verbatim from the description: "under certain request mixes (short chat turns mixed with long-prefills) we see tail latency spikes and unfair slowdown of latency-sensitive routes... The goal is to reduce 99.9th token latency for latency-sensitive routes by 35-50% without losing >10% aggregate throughput on heavy mixed workloads."
rows.method:
Cast wide with BM25 on the question's own wording and immediately learned the corpus vocabulary: it is a synthetic enterprise corpus for "Redwood Inference", where this topic lives as Linear tickets about prefill/decode scheduling, continuous batching, tail latency, TTFT/TPOT. The hazard was that the corpus contains roughly a hundred near-duplicate scheduler tickets, each with a slightly different goal line (p99 decode -20% / throughput 5%, p99 -25% / 6%, p95 decode -25% / 7%, p99 decode -40% / 2%, and so on). Prose querying could not discriminate among them.

The breakthrough was discovering that the tokenizer preserves literal percent tokens, so "10%" works as a term inside the `all` (AND) mode. I then used the question's one hard numeric constraint - throughput loss under about ten percent - as a filter rather than as prose, ANDing "10%" against p99 / decode / prefill / interactive / throughput / loss / reduce. That collapsed the candidate set from ~100 to 8, and the first read of ENG-23109 hit the exact sentence. I also tried ANDing "10%" together with guessed reduction figures ("30%", "40%") to exploit the fact that the needle sentence contains two numbers; that was useful for ranking even though the true figure was a 35-50% range.

Along the way I ruled out several strong decoys by reading them in full: ENG-887776 TokenFlow Divider (>=25% p99 for latency-tier, throughput degradation <=6%, acceptance "no >10% throughput loss"), ENG-34678 hybrid priority queue (p99 decode >=20%, throughput within 5%), ENG-22670 prefill-decode orchestrator (p99 decode >=40%, throughput regression <=2%), ENG-9534 (p99 decode >=30%, <=5%), ENG-219307 (P95 >=25%, throughput loss <5%), ENG-554321 (P99 >=25%, <5%), ENG-51674 (p95 decode >=25%, tokens/sec drop <=7%), and the entire ENG-2417 mixed-workload-scheduler initiative plus PM-612 (p95 TTFT >=15%, throughput guardrail 3-5%), which matches the "short/long prompt mix" framing but targets TTFT/e2e p95, not per-token latency, and uses a much tighter throughput budget.

ENG-23109 is the unique document pairing all three elements of the question: the short-chat-plus-long-prefill mix, a worst-case PER-TOKEN metric (99.9th token latency, not TTFT and not end-to-end), and the ~10% aggregate throughput bound.

Cast wide with BM25 on the question's mechanism (GPU serving, tail latency, attention kernel fallback, scratch/workspace growth), then switched to the corpus's own vocabulary once it surfaced: "kernel chooser", "kernel selector", "transient headroom", "workspace_exceeded", "kernel_routing_reason", "fallback_rate", "pre_reserve_mb", "flash -> cuBLASLt/Triton/paged/sdpa". Used phrase() to test candidate answer-shapes (chunked prefill, varlen/unpadded, length bucketing, hysteresis, sticky kernel, pre-reserve, workspace inflation, transient scratch) and all() conjunctions to narrow (skew+kernel+latency+scratch, pad+variance+kernel+p99, mixed+lengths+p99+flash+reserve, loadgen+skew+kernel+p99). Used src() to map the corpus layout (slack/eng-runtime, google_drive/shared_drives/engineering/serving-runtime, github/redwood PRs, linear ENG tickets, confluence/eng-serving-runtime) and near() to pull sibling chunks of the most promising doc. Read 14 full documents in the dense serving-runtime cluster.

GPU inference runtime = the `redwood` repo's serving runtime. The change was PR #21807, "dynamic-scratch-reuse-and-fanout-aware-kernel-selection-to-reduce-peak-gpu-workspace" (author Maya Chen, opened 2026-02-18, merged 2026-02-23, branch feature/dynamic-scratch-fanout-kernels).

It introduced two complementary mechanisms; the one that targets the worst-case transient spike is DYNAMIC SCRATCH REUSE: a runtime scratch allocator (new `runtime/scratch_manager.{cpp,h}`) with a lock-free free-list per size-class and lifetime-tagging. It tracks short-lived temp regions by lifetime buckets and reuses buffers across operators within the same execution frame, instead of each kernel allocating its own per-op temp buffer. The scratch allocation path was hooked into the kernel interface and the critical kernels -- attention, rotary, layernorm -- were modified to request scratch via the manager. The kernel interface signature was extended with an optional `scratch_token` that defaults to nullptr, so it is backward compatible.

The second, complementary mechanism is FANOUT-AWARE KERNEL SELECTION: a fanout heuristic in `runtime/kernel_selector.cpp` that uses observed Q*K fanout counters (collected per model) to choose between tiled/packed attention kernels and low-memory fused attention kernels, trading compute for lower transient memory. A compatibility path keeps models pinned to older kernel profiles on the legacy selector.

Motivation stated in the PR: high peak GPU workspace for mixed-sequence inference (short+long requests) and multi-query fanout workloads, where existing arena tuning plus static activation checkpointing still left (1) transient scratch buffer spikes from kernels that allocate per-op temp buffers and (2) suboptimal kernel choices as operator fanout changes.

Measured results: on A100-40GB with a GPT-2 style 1B-param model and a mixed workload (50% seq_len=32, 50% seq_len=1024), peak workspace dropped from 16.8GB to 12.1GB (~28% reduction). For high-fanout Q=16 tests the transient peak fell ~34% when the fanout-aware kernel was selected. Cost: median latency for long requests rose ~2.3% in the worst-case knob-on scenario where the low-memory kernel is chosen; a policy-level config flag exposes the latency-vs-memory preference.

Rollout: gated behind `runtime.scratch_reuse.enabled=false` by default in the PR, with a phased plan (non-production clusters for 2 weeks, then opt-in for Dedicated clusters under memory pressure, then flip the default after a week of metrics). The kernel heuristic is additive and disableable via `runtime.kernel_selector.fanout_heuristic=false`. New telemetry: `runtime.scratch_reuse.alloc_reuse_ratio`, `kernel_selector.fanout_decision_count`, `memory.scratch_peak_by_model`. Benchmarks added under benchmark-lab/ including `fanout_memory_profile.py` and an e2e memory test simulating interleaved short/long requests. The PR deliberately did not change global arena sizing heuristics; that was deferred to follow-up ENG-1919.

Root cause: the customer's transit provider made a perimeter firewall/policy change on 2026-03-11 that rate-limits and drops ICMP Type 3 Code 4 ("Fragmentation Needed") under heavy NAT. Path MTU Discovery depends on those ICMP messages, so once they stopped being delivered, any TCP segment larger than the true path MTU with DF set was silently blackholed — a PMTU blackhole.

Why it hits exactly this traffic shape: the private deployment (FinData Analytics' customer-managed VPC, peered to the Redwood control plane via TGW, worker nodes at default MTU 1500) fetches model shards from presigned S3 URLs using HTTP/2 multiplexed range requests and long-lived gRPC/HTTP2 connections. Those push large frames/TLS records, so they exceed path MTU where small requests and embedding flows never do. The observable signature is: TLS handshake completes, HTTP/2 SETTINGS/HEADERS exchange succeeds, a few KB of DATA frames arrive, then the stream is left half-open with no further DATA and no ACK progression past a certain MSS-sized segment, timing out around 30s with serving-runtime gRPC code 14 UNAVAILABLE and downstream ECONNRESET. Captures at three points (worker VM, customer edge router, provider egress) showed the ICMP type 3 code 4 being generated at the edge router but disappearing at the provider handoff.

Why lowering the node MTU fixes it instantly: setting worker MTU to 1400 makes every packet fit inside the real path MTU, so PMTUD never needs to run and the missing ICMP signal stops mattering. Streaming resumes immediately. The equivalent alternative mitigation is capping server-side TLS record size (tested at 1200) or server-side chunking, which requires a runtime change. The permanent fix is on the provider: customer opened transit-provider ticket TP-44821 to allow ICMP Type 3 Code 4 / restore PMTU transparency. Control-plane auth and presigned URL generation were explicitly ruled out — working presigned URLs still stall when path MTU issues are present.

Root cause: during the 2025-04-11 NovusTech / Redwood Inference incident (impact window ~07:39Z-10:05Z, mitigation applied 09:25 PDT), a memory-pressure cascade on the westus-edge-3 shard group -- triggered by long-context interactive streams combined with a recent model change that increased per-token KV-cache size -- pushed KV usage past a threshold. Affected shards then entered a backpressure state that DEFERRED TOKEN EMISSION until a background eviction/GC cycle ran, so tokens arrived in big bursts separated by 15-30 second gaps. Roughly 12% of live streaming capacity sat on those shards; ~60% of the customer's active sessions showed degraded UX and one voice agent dropped mid-conversation.

Immediate workaround recommended (Stephanie Nguyen, 08:40 PDT, framed as low-friction / non-code): set a CLIENT-SIDE STREAMING TIMEOUT OF 10s WITH ONE AUTO-RETRY -- explicitly "this avoids long blackouts and keeps sessions responsive." Alongside it she recommended falling back to the non-streaming /generate endpoint for mission-critical flows, and reducing max_tokens_per_call by 30% for long-context sessions to slow KV-cache growth. Server side, Redwood rolled temporary-config.patch to cap per-session KV at 30MB on westus-edge-3, enabled aggressive prefix-cache TTLs for 90 minutes, and warm-routed ~8% of the tenant's traffic to dedicated non-streaming nodes for 2 hours.

SUP-672839 (Jira, customer-support), "Accept-queue buildup from ephemeral prewarm handshake triggering sustained 5xx wave" — Acme Retail, dedicated tier, prod:us-east, 2026-03-12/13, Sev1/P1, reporter Maya Chen, assignee Diego Alvarez.

Cause: two mechanisms compounding on the same trigger. At ~23:10 UTC a high-concurrency burst from Acme's client brought many long-lived streaming chat connections at the same time as a bulk embedding upload job (redwood-open-7B for chat, acme-embedder-v2 for embeddings).

1) Warmup connection churn: the ephemeral runtime prewarm subsystem launched warmup workers that performed many short TLS handshakes against the proxy/acceptor layer. Concurrently the autoscaler scaled IN on memory-utilization thresholds, so warmers were being torn down while new warmers spun up. That window produced handshake storms / SYN backpressure at the acceptor — SYN_RECV/SYN_SENT queue growth, orphan and half-open sockets, "handshake timeout" TLS renegotiation failures in ephemeral-proxy, api-gateway accept() latency spikes and "backlog exceeded", with net.core.somaxconn at default and hitting its limit on several nodes. New connections saw delayed accept or early RST, and the gateway returned 502/503 "upstream unavailable". Scale-in events correlate with the start of the 5xx staircase (Hypothesis B, partial evidence).

2) Disk-backed cache write pressure: the serving runtime's KV-cache checkpointing/snapshotting issued frequent small writes to local NVMe, causing write amplification and elevated NVMe write latency/iowait. That delayed worker threads, which increased connection hold time and fed further accept-queue growth, plus runtime evictions and OOM-suppress warnings shortly after each prewarm wave (Hypothesis C, strong evidence — correlated NVMe latency spikes and runtime evictions).

Hypothesis A (gateway threadpool starvation from large-sidecar healthchecks) was ruled out; thread-pool metrics stayed normal. Kernel backlog tuning was noted as relief, not root cause.

Impact: ~12% 5xx on streaming chat routes at peak, +400ms p95 tail latency, customer-visible message truncation and reconnect loops.

Mitigations: routed Acme traffic to a reserved warm pool (5xx 12% -> ~1.5-1.8% within 3 minutes), cut prewarm concurrency 8 -> 2 per node, disabled aggressive KV-cache snapshotting for the affected runtime group, raised somaxconn on edge acceptors. Permanent remediation: ENG-998 (autoscaler avoids scale-in during active prewarm for dedicated tenants), RUNTIME-1421 (prewarm handshake exponential backoff + connection reuse), RUNTIME-1422 (KV-cache snapshot batching with async fsync to cut small-file NVMe write amplification), OPS-776 (accept backlog / tcp_max_syn_backlog tuning), MON-312 (alert correlating prewarm spawn rate, NVMe iowait, accept queue depth).

The answering document is gene c03443853bd5fcac — "Longform reading scrapbook: compression, KV heuristics, and RAG probes" (Hector Alvarez, eng-applied-ml, 2027-06-18, users/hector-alvarez-longform-reading-scratch-2027-06-18.json).

Its framing matches the question: KV cache is described as the biggest latency/cost lever "for long-context use-cases at serving time", with the rule of thumb that high compression on old turns (>= N tokens back) is acceptable while near-term KV entries need much higher fidelity — i.e. older context aggressively compressed to relieve GPU DRAM/memory-bandwidth pressure.

Under "RAG instability notes (various conference talks + community threads)" it states: when retrieval and compressed KV interact, the model often overfits to compressed-context artifacts, and "hallucinations often start at hallucinated citation tokens (weird markers)" — the tendency to start making up references right after a retrieval step.

The suggested mitigation (verbatim intent): "Practical mitigation: calibrated retrieval scoring (confidence-aware masking), hallucination detectors that watch for sudden entropy drops, and short-term cache reset after retrieval events."

So the three-part mitigation is: (1) calibrated / confidence-aware retrieval scoring with masking, (2) hallucination detectors that watch for sudden entropy drops, and (3) a short-term cache reset immediately after retrieval events.

A closely related but distinct mitigation appears in gene d562883da7dcb8fb (Kai Morgan, context-stitching paper-curation memo): for the drift/hallucination problem when compressed KVs lose precise referents, include provenance tokens (chunk-id markers) plus a cheap citation mechanism so the model can say "I might be recalling from chunk #5". Gene 9f5386fe448180a8 (Elena Morales KV-compression sprint) documents the same failure ("compressed cold-chunk lost citations -> hallucinated reference numbers") but proposes a different fix (splitting compression into semantics-first vs tokens-first pathways for factual anchoring).
